parole.significato: That rules the stars.
parole.testo: From Latin astripotens, likely through Middle French astripotent.

parole.significato: A participant in any of a group of sporting activities including track and field, road running, cross country running a…
parole.testo: From Middle English athlete, from Latin āthlēta (and probably also partly from Middle French athlete), from Ancient Greek ἀθλητής (athlētḗs), from ἀθλέω (athléō, “compete for a prize”), from ἆθλον (âthlon, “prize”) or ἆθλος (âthlos, “competition”).

parole.significato: One who has been captured or is otherwise confined.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English captif; derived from Latin captīvus, probably through a borrowing from a Middle French intermediate. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“seize, hold”). Doublet of caitiff.

parole.significato: Synonym of scaphoid abdomen.
parole.testo: From Latin carinatus, from carina (“keel”), + Middle French abdomen, from Latin abdomen, possibly from abdō (“conceal”), from ab (“away”) + dere (“to put, place”).

parole.significato: Synonym of Chaldean.
parole.testo: From Latin chaldaeus via Middle French Chaldee.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, resembling or living in a cloister.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin claustrālis (“of the cloister”), probably via Middle French cloistral. Doublet of claustral.

parole.significato: Corresponding; suitable; adapted; congruous.
parole.testo: From Latin, via Middle French or directly, from Medieval Latin correspondēns, present participle of correspondeō.

parole.significato: Having round or blunt teeth on its margin; scalloped.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin crēnātus, merged with a Latinization of Middle French crené, past participle of crener (“to mark with a notch”), derivative of cren, cran (“notch”), of Celtic origin.

parole.significato: The act of dissecting.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dissectiōnem, perhaps via Middle French dissection. By surface analysis, dissect + -ion.

parole.significato: To urge, press (someone); to insist on, demand (something).
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin īnstāre; its precise evolution is uncertain. OED hints at (unattested) Middle French *instanter.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or resembling the Moon (that is, Luna, the Earth's moon).
parole.testo: From Middle English lunar (“shaped like the crescent moon”), from Latin lūnāris (“of or pertaining to the moon, lunar”) (possibly through Middle French lunaire (modern French lunaire (“lunar”)), from lūna (“the Moon; crescent shape”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“bright; to shine”))

parole.significato: Synonym of purify, to ritually cleanse or renew, particularly to do so with a propitiatory offering or (historical) the…
parole.testo: From Latin lustrātus (“lustrated”), perfect passive participle of lustrō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from lustrum (“ritual purification”) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix), q.v. In reference to imparting luster, further via senses of Middle French lustre, from Old Italian lustro.

parole.significato: Working wonders; wonderful.
parole.testo: From Latin mirificus and Middle French mirifique.

parole.significato: A symbol that is not a word and represents a number, such as the Arabic numerals 1, 2, 3 or the Roman numerals I, V, X,…
parole.testo: As an adjective, from Middle English numeral, numerall, from Latin numerālis (“pertaining to a number”), from numerus (“a number”). As a noun, via Middle French numeral.

parole.significato: Of, similar to, or related to papyrus.
parole.testo: From Latin papȳrāceus (“made of papyrus”) under influence of Middle French papyracee and French papiracé.

parole.significato: A planetree.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin platanus; later reborrowed from Middle French platane.

parole.significato: A plebeian, a member of the lower class of Roman citizens.
parole.testo: From Latin plēbs (“the plebeian class”), probably via Middle French plebe (“plebeians, commoners, the rabble”) and possibly later understood as a clipping of plebeian. Cognate with Italian plebe, Spanish plebe, Portuguese plebe.

parole.significato: Capable of being accomplished; feasible.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin prācticābilis, partly modelled on Middle French praticable. By surface analysis, practice (verb) + -able.

parole.significato: Act of healing or curing.
parole.testo: From Middle English sanacion, sanacioun, from Latin sānātiō (“a healing”) and Middle French sanacion.

parole.significato: suspicion
parole.testo: From Middle English suspeccion, suspeccioun, suspeccyon, suspectyon, susspeccioun, from Latin suspectiō and Middle French suspeccion, suspection. Doublet of soupçon. By surface analysis, suspect + -ion.

parole.significato: Relating to, or skilled in, theory; theoretical.
parole.testo: From Middle English theoryk, from Latin theōricus and Middle French theorique. By surface analysis, theory + -ic.
